(CNN) — Filmmaker Michael Moore, whose new documentary, *Sicko*, examines America’s health-care system, faced off Tuesday with CNN chief medical correspondent and practicing neurosurgeon Dr. Sanjay Gupta.

Moore and Gupta argued over a report Gupta aired Monday on CNN about *Sicko*. Appearing on CNN’s *Larry King Live*, Moore criticized the segment, saying Gupta had claimed the film’s facts were inaccurate.

“He said the facts were fudged,” Moore said, referring to Gupta. “That’s a lie. None of the facts are fudged.”

The two shouted and debated the data cited in Gupta’s report and in Moore’s film. Moore said his staff had provided Gupta with documentation supporting the film’s facts before the report aired, and accused Gupta of broadcasting the segment despite knowing his own facts were wrong. Gupta denied that claim.

“We try and look for some of the best sources we can possibly find,” Gupta said. “Michael has a lot of different numbers. ... You’re sort of cherry-picking data from different reports.”

Both men, however, agreed on the central premise of *Sicko*: that America’s health-care system is beset by serious problems and needs reform.

“I thought it was a good movie, and I wanted to say that,” Gupta said. “I think it strikes at the irrefutable fact — it’s broken. We get it.”

Gupta also praised Moore for bringing greater attention to the issue.

Still, Gupta said he was concerned that the film — which notes that other developed nations, including France and Canada, have universal health care — could leave audiences with the impression that health care in those countries is free. Although patients may not pay for services at a doctor’s office, Gupta noted, they pay high taxes to fund such systems, a point he worried *Sicko* viewers might not fully understand.

Moore responded that Americans pay more through copays, deductibles and insurance premiums.

“We [America] have a system built on profit,” the filmmaker said.

Moore then asked Gupta whether the current system, which requires him to obtain approval from an insurance company before performing certain procedures, is cumbersome.

“It’s a shameful system, especially when I’m dealing with some of my patients,” Gupta said.

But Gupta questioned Moore’s apparent solution: placing health care in the hands of the Bush administration, which Moore has fiercely criticized in the past, particularly in his film *Fahrenheit 9/11*.

“The government actually used to do things right,” Moore responded. “The problem is who we put in power.”

Moore, who has adamantly opposed the war in Iraq, said the government should reprioritize — a position he had taken years before skepticism about the war’s success became widespread in Washington.

“I am sorry we’ve taken so much time trying to correct [Gupta’s] facts here tonight instead of talking about the real issue” — the ailing health-care system, Moore said.

(CNN) — Michael Moore, the filmmaker behind the new documentary *Sicko*, which critiques the U.S. health care system, clashed Tuesday with CNN’s chief medical correspondent, Dr. Sanjay Gupta, a practicing neurosurgeon.

The dispute centered on a CNN report Gupta had presented Monday about Moore’s film. Appearing on CNN’s *Larry King Live*, Moore objected to Gupta’s characterization of the documentary.

“He said the facts were fudged,” Moore said, referring to Gupta. “That’s a lie. None of the facts are fudged.”

During the exchange, Moore and Gupta argued loudly over the statistics each had relied on. Moore said members of his team had provided Gupta with documentation supporting the movie’s claims before the report was broadcast, and he accused Gupta of airing the segment despite knowing his information was incorrect. Gupta denied that accusation.

“We try and look for some of the best sources we can possibly find,” Gupta said. “Michael has a lot of different numbers. ... You’re sort of cherry-picking data from different reports.”

Despite their disagreement, both men accepted the central argument of *Sicko*: that the American health care system has serious flaws and requires repair.

“I thought it was a good movie, and I wanted to say that,” Gupta said. “I think it strikes at the irrefutable fact — it’s broken. We get it.” He also credited Moore with bringing more public attention to the issue.

Gupta said, however, that he worried the film could leave viewers with the impression that health care in other developed countries, including France and Canada, is free because those nations provide universal coverage. He pointed out that even if patients do not pay at the doctor’s office, they help finance the system through higher taxes, a point he feared audiences might miss.

Moore countered that Americans already pay heavily through co-payments, deductibles and insurance premiums. “We [America] have a system built on profit,” he said.

He then asked Gupta whether he finds the current system burdensome, given that it sometimes requires him to get permission from an insurance company before carrying out certain medical procedures.

“It’s a shameful system, especially when I’m dealing with some of my patients,” Gupta replied.

Still, Gupta challenged what he saw as Moore’s proposed answer: handing responsibility for health care to the Bush administration, which Moore had sharply attacked before, most notably in his film *Fahrenheit 9/11*.

“The government actually used to do things right,” Moore answered. “The problem is who we put in power.”

Moore, a strong opponent of the Iraq war, said the government should change its priorities — a stance he had taken long before doubts about the war’s success became widespread in Washington.

“I am sorry we’ve taken so much time trying to correct [Gupta’s] facts here tonight instead of talking about the real issue” — the struggling health care system, Moore said.

Gupta acknowledged that U.S. health care is costly and leaves many people uninsured or underinsured, but maintained that Moore’s film simplified complex systems and omitted some drawbacks of government-run or universal health-care models.

Host Larry King moderated the back-and-forth, giving both men time to respond as they challenged each other’s sources and interpretations.

*Sicko*, released in 2007, became one of Moore’s most prominent documentaries and helped intensify public debate over health-care reform in the United States. # Michael Moore Defends *Sicko* Against Sanjay Gupta’s Fact-Checking Claims

When Michael Moore released *Sicko* in 2007, the documentary quickly became one of the most visible and polarizing critiques of the American health care system. Unlike Moore’s earlier films, *Sicko* did not focus primarily on people without insurance; instead, it centered on insured Americans who still faced denied claims, crushing bills, bureaucratic hurdles, and life-threatening gaps in coverage.

The film’s central argument was blunt: the United States spends enormous sums on health care while leaving many patients vulnerable, and it should look more seriously at systems in countries that provide universal coverage.

That argument drew strong reactions, including from CNN’s chief medical correspondent, Dr. Sanjay Gupta, who aired a fact-check segment accusing Moore of cherry-picking evidence and “fudging” some facts. Moore responded forcefully, defending the film’s accuracy and accusing CNN of missing the broader point: that American health care was failing millions of people.

## Gupta’s Criticism of *Sicko*

Gupta’s critique did not reject the idea that the U.S. health care system had deep problems. In fact, he agreed that American health care was troubled and in need of reform. But he argued that *Sicko* presented an overly selective picture.

Among Gupta’s concerns were that Moore compared health care systems in ways that favored his argument, highlighted positive aspects of countries such as Canada, Britain, France, and Cuba while downplaying their shortcomings, and used statistics that Gupta said were incomplete or misleading.

The phrase that received the most attention was Gupta’s claim that Moore had “fudged the facts.” For Moore, that accusation was especially serious because it challenged not just his interpretation, but the credibility of the documentary itself.

## Moore’s Response

Moore pushed back aggressively. He argued that *Sicko* was thoroughly researched and that its facts were backed by publicly available sources, including government and international data. Moore and his team posted responses online addressing CNN’s claims point by point, saying Gupta had either misunderstood the film’s numbers or relied on flawed comparisons.

Moore also appeared on CNN to confront the criticism directly. In an interview with Wolf Blitzer, he criticized CNN for presenting Gupta’s segment as a neutral fact-check while, in Moore’s view, failing to account for the role of private insurance companies and corporate interests in shaping the U.S. system.

Later, Moore and Gupta discussed the issue together on *Larry King Live*. The exchange was tense but revealing: Gupta stood by his view that the film was selective in some places, while Moore insisted that the documentary’s claims were accurate and that any debate over individual numbers should not distract from the suffering caused by the American system.

## The Cuba Controversy

One of the most controversial parts of *Sicko* involved Moore taking a group of 9/11 rescue workers to Cuba, where they received medical attention. Moore used the sequence to contrast the difficulty some Americans faced in getting care at home with the treatment they received abroad.

Critics argued that Cuba was an especially problematic example because its health care system exists within an authoritarian political structure and because foreigners or politically favored patients may receive better treatment than ordinary Cuban citizens. Moore responded that the point was not to portray Cuba as a political model, but to show that even a much poorer country could provide certain kinds of care at far lower cost.

For Moore, the Cuba segment was a moral provocation: if the United States could spend vast sums on health care and still leave sick workers struggling, then something was fundamentally wrong.

## A Shared Diagnosis: The U.S. System Is Broken

Despite their sharp disagreement, Moore and Gupta shared an important premise: American health care was broken.

Gupta acknowledged that the system had serious failures, including high costs, uneven access, and poor outcomes in some areas despite the country’s medical wealth and technological sophistication. Moore’s film made the same broad case, but in a more confrontational and emotional style.

Their dispute was less about whether the system needed reform and more about how to argue for it. Moore believed the crisis was so severe that the film needed to expose the human consequences of a profit-driven insurance system. Gupta argued that documentaries still had an obligation to present comparisons carefully and not gloss over problems in other countries’ systems.

## The Larger Debate

The clash between Moore and Gupta captured a larger tension in American health care debates. Supporters of *Sicko* saw the film as a necessary indictment of a system that left patients at the mercy of insurers and medical bills. Critics saw it as persuasive but one-sided, arguing that universal health care systems abroad also face challenges such as wait times, rationing concerns, taxation burdens, and capacity limits.

Still, *Sicko* helped bring health care reform into mainstream conversation at a crucial moment, just a few years before the passage of the Affordable Care Act. It gave emotional force to questions policymakers were already debating: Why does the United States spend so much while achieving uneven results? Why do insured people still go bankrupt from medical costs? Should health care be treated as a right rather than a commodity?

## Conclusion

Michael Moore’s defense of *Sicko* against Sanjay Gupta’s criticisms was not just a dispute over statistics. It was a clash over storytelling, evidence, and the best way to confront a national crisis.

Gupta argued that Moore cherry-picked and overstated parts of the case. Moore replied that the film’s facts were sound and that CNN was focusing on technical objections while ignoring the deeper scandal of American health care.

But beneath the argument, both men agreed on the central issue: the U.S. health care system was failing too many people. Their debate reflected the broader national struggle over how to describe that failure — and what kind of reform would be bold enough to fix it.

Host Larry King repeatedly moved the conversation back to the central question raised by *Sicko*: whether health care should be considered a right.

Moore answered emphatically that it should. Gupta agreed that Americans should not be left without care, but stopped short of endorsing Moore’s preferred solution.

The segment reflected a larger national debate that has intensified as health care costs continue to rise and millions of Americans struggle with medical expenses. Moore’s film became a flashpoint not only because of its criticism of insurers and drug companies, but because it challenged the idea that market-based health care can provide fair and affordable treatment for all.

While the two men remained sharply divided over the film’s accuracy and conclusions, both acknowledged that the U.S. system leaves many patients vulnerable — and that major reform is needed.
